articles.text: Mountain View Cemetery is inviting the community to attend the 18th Annual Tulip Exhibition at the cemetery’s Tower Chapel, this Friday through Sunday, March 20-22, from 10 a.m. - 4 p.m. This free event welcomes Spring with floral arrangements by Bay Area florists, garden clubs, and students from a college floral design class. Photographers, florists, flower enthusiasts, and nature and art lovers are welcome. Since its inception in 2006, the cemetery’s annual tulip exhibit has become a cherished community tradition. Under the guidance of Special Events Coordinator Kristie Ly, this year is the exhibit’s third year back after a hiatus due to COVID-19 restrictions. “A must-see free event for all nature, plant, and floral enthusiasts alike,” said Ly. Following the exhibition, guests may enjoy a Pop-up Arts Show at J. Miller Flowers to celebrate its 56th year. The pop-up show will take place from 11 a.m. - 3 p.m. Mountain View Cemetery (5000 Piedmont Avenue) is a historic garden cemetery in the foothills of Oakland and Piedmont. One of the oldest cemeteries in the Western U.S., it has served the community since 1863 and even includes a section for Civil War soldiers. For more information on the cemetery or its annual tulip exhibition, visit www.mountainviewcemetery.org. articles.text: The City Council will review a proposed framework for soliciting and evaluating developers interested in building housing in the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan area and provide direction to staff on ranking criteria, review process, and other priorities at their regular meeting on Monday, March 16. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, adopted in October 2025, provides a vision and framework for the construction of 132 new homes on City-owned land along Moraga Avenue, including road safety improvements, design and landscaping standards, and wildfire safety requirements. The next step to implementing the Specific Plan is for the City to identify a developer to partner with. City staff is proposing to issue a Request for Qualifications (RFQ) for potential developers this spring. This would solicit detailed information on the financial capability and experience of interested firms, as well as their general conceptual plans for development. This approach aims to generate a large pool of well-qualified developers while maintaining local control and ensuring quality future development. A review committee consisting of both senior City staff and subject matter experts in relevant fields, such as real estate finance, housing development, land use planning, or architecture, would evaluate responses and make a recommendation to City Council. The City would then enter into an exclusive negotiating agreement with the selected firm. At Monday’s meeting, Council will review the proposed framework for the RFQ and provide direction to staff on ranking criteria, review committee membership, preferred approach to the transfer of City-owned land, and any other Council priorities. Presentation materials will be available on the project website after the meeting. The Moraga Canyon Specific Plan is available for download at piedmont.ca.gov/ MCSP.
articles.title: City Council considers framework for soliciting Moraga Canyon developers

articles.text: From 2020-2023, catalytic converter theft was a huge driver of crime in Piedmont and the region. In recent years, the regional enforcement has helped reduce the numbers, but it’s still a threat that any resident could encounter. The catalytic converter, or “cat,” is an emissions component, usually located on the belly of the car; exhaust flows into it before going to the muffler. A cat uses rare earth metals in a chemical reaction to convert nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, and hydrocarbons into less hazardous substances such as carbon dioxide, water vapor, and nitrogen gas. The catalyst in your converter is typically made of palladium (Pd), rhodium (Rh), and platinum (Pt). These rare earth metals are what thieves are targeting. articles.text: Ella Rey Nash is a local musician born and raised in Piedmont, who dreams of one day headlining her own tour. She has decided to pursue her passion and put her all into making a dream a reality. Nash, who describes her music as indie pop, is currently releasing one song a month, with the most recent single out titled “Simple Life.” Her next single will be released on Friday, March 27, titled “2 a.m. in Texas.” She records with a producer in Oakland and San Francisco. A PHS grad in 2020, Ella has been heavily involved in music her entire life. Throughout high school, she’d been in Piedmont choirs, the acapella program, and multiple musical and dance performances. “I was very drawn to anything music from pretty early on, and was kind of always writing,” said Nash. During the COVID-19 lockdown, Nash had a lot of time on her hands, so she began to write. She became addicted to telling stories through songs. “I think the songwriting part of my brain really clicked into place for the first time. Up until then, I was always writing, but I never really finished any of my songs and didn’t take any of them too seriously,” Nash continued. “But during COVID, I realized I could write a song and finish it and keep doing that over and over. I think that was when I realized. ‘Okay, I could do this.’” Nash’s song “Simple Life” is the first release of a six-song rollout and highlights her ambition. It’s inspired by her idea of how society teaches us to pursue certain goals in our lives, and how Nash’s ambitions may not fit. She wants more. As an independent artist, Nash has to work extra hard to get her songs noticed. “It’s very overwhelming,” she said. “There’s a never-ending list of things I could always be doing at any given minute. You’re kind of just always feeling it out and putting out new music and seeing what sticks with people, and learning as you go.” Thankfully for Nash, she’s found a strong community in the Bay Area and in Piedmont that has supported her creative endeavors. She works with a local producer and still writes songs Nash performing on stage with her friends as she did in high school. As an independent artist, your best friend is social media. The biggest for musical discovery is the social media platform TikTok. According to the platform’s Year-End Music Report in 2024, 84% of the songs that reached Billboard’s Global 200 last year went viral first on TikTok. Nash has embraced this idea and is on her “posting grind.” “My mindset is, every time I post, I’m trying to get the video or the photo or whatever, in front of new people each time,” she added. “I feel like social media is kind of today’s version of being on the radio. To be a big deal is [when] your song is going viral as a TikTok sound.” Ella’s goal for music is to one day go on tour either as an opener for another musician or on her own. She’s also passionate about the idea of writing music for television or movies. “I got a lot of my inspiration from movies and TV, and I think it would be kind of a cool challenge to have to write for something more specific,” she mentioned. In the pursuit of her creative dreams, she hopes others can be The cover photo for Nash’s single “Simple Life” inspired by her goals and pursue their own dreams as well. “I tried for a long time, tried to convince myself that I didn’t want to pursue this, because I don’t think I believed in myself enough,” Nash continued. “Once I released my first song, I realized that there is no world where I’m happy if I don’t try and do this. I think you just really have to listen to your gut. No one is going to walk into your life and tell you, ‘Okay, it’s time to pursue your dream now.’ If you want it bad enough, you can make it happen.” Those interested in finding Nash’s music can find her on platforms such as Spotify, Apple Music, and YouTube. Superintendent Dear PUSD Families & Staff: In my recent State of the District report, I raised several questions regarding our use of technology for learning at all grade levels. Over the last year, I have been considering the many promises made about EdTech, especially in light of recent research on cell phone and device use, including work by Jonathan Haidt and Jared Horvath. Both question the impact of technology on our children. While we have a strong record of students who achieve academically and socially, we must re-examine our use of technology and how constant connectivity, both inside and outside the classroom, impacts the experience of our students. To address emerging questions, I have recommended a comprehensive technology audit of our technology use. Through my meetings with our teachers, staff, and parents, I appreciate just how complex the uses of technology have become across our district. The audit will examine our backend infrastructure, staffing, data analysis, and student screen time and purpose. The timing is particularly appropriate as we are currently revising our District Technology Plan. We are still defining the final scope to determine which components require an outside consultant and which will be handled internally, as an external audit may not fully capture the nuances of individual classroom instruction. Given the decade-long development of our current systems, decoupling technology from our learning environment cannot happen overnight. Any changes must be the result of a thoughtful, evidence-based analysis involving our entire school community. As a first step, we are bringing a contract for a professional technology audit firm to the Board for approval at the March 18th meeting. We look forward to collaborating with our staff and families to ensure our technology use their digital training manuals with every team in the land, ensuring that as they grew, they pulled the whole community up with them. Through my meetings with our teachers, staff, and parents, I appreciate just how complex the uses of technology have become across our district. The audit will examine our backend infrastructure, staffing, data analysis, and student screen time and purpose. The timing is particularly appropriate as we are currently revising our District Technology Plan. We are still defining the final scope to determine which components require an outside consultant and which will be handled internally, as an external audit may not fully capture the nuances of individual classroom instruction. Robots have played a pivotal role in helping humans learn more about space. The Cassini spacecraft is a complex autonomous robot, meaning it can work by itself! Using computers and powerful antennas, scientists sent commands from Earth for Cassini to complete. A great example of this is the launch of the Huygens probe in 2005. The Huygens probe, which was aboard the Cassini spacecraft when it launched, went to the surface of Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. pages.text: Wednesday, March 18, 2026 9 City to Snow Continued from page 8 there, we rushed over to SnoVentures, where Palisades Tahoe had generously donated tubing tickets to our group. After the kids were suited up in their snow gear donated by Sports Basement, we spent the next hour yelling, spinning, and laughing as the group slid down the tracks using big inflatable innertubes. When the tubing session was over, some kids made snow angels while others tried hiking or sledding in Olympic Valley. Two BGCO members did a fantastic job building their first snowman, which West Oakland Branch leader Rodney Cook proudly guarded to make sure it didn’t get accidentally damaged in the continued snowplay. After enjoying our delicious Mulberry’s lunch, we drove to Donner Memorial State Park which had donated parking passes for our vehicles. The kids marched to the monument, took pictures, and played a little more in the snow. Then we moved inside the Donner Memorial Museum to participate in a scavenger hunt which made it even more fun. Finally, after determining the winners, we all said our goodbyes, and the BGCO van headed back to Oakland with snacks and drinks donated by the Oakland Grocery Outlet. When I met with the BGCO members the following week to show them pictures from the trip, they all said the trip was “very fun,” they loved their scout helpers, and “definitely would do this trip again.” (Thanks to Nevaeh, Kei’lani, Love, and Ma’layah for their comments and feedback). Tiquan even called the trip “existentially great.” Everybody agreed that whether it is in the snow or in Oakland, we all wanted to see each other again. articles.text: Join Disability Rights Education and Defense Fund (DREDF) advocate Andrea Yu for a comprehensive look at the IEP process from start to finish. On Wednesday, March 25, from 7 - 8:30 p.m., Andrea will host a virtual walk-through on Zoom. The talk will teach parents how to navigate the IEP document, and practical steps families can take when the process isn’t working as it should. The session will also explore the foundational principles of the IDEA, covering key concepts such as free appropriate public education, the least restrictive environment, the right to an independent educational evaluation, and what meaningful parental participation truly looks like. Andrea Yu is an Education Advocate at DREDF, a leading national civil rights law and policy center founded in 1979 and directed by individuals with disabilities and parents of children with disabilities. Andrea brings seven years of hands-on school experience to her role, having worked as an afterschool program leader, preschool teacher assistant, and special education paraprofessional. Through that work, she discovered a deep passion for supporting students with disabilities and their families, a calling that led her to become a special education preschool teacher. She remains dedicated to the students and families she has worked with and looks forward to extending that impact to more communities through DREDF. articles.text: Piedmont High’s softball team pulled off a dominant 16-6 win over American on Friday, March 13 at the Witter Softball Field, improving its record to 3-2 overall. Things started slowly after trailing 2-0 deficit through the top of the second inning. But the Highlanders stormed back with three runs in the bottom of the second and exploded for nine runs in the bottom of the third. They closed the game by way of the 10-run rule by adding three runs in the bottom of the sixth. “It’s a young team. The first inning was rough but they settled down and started playing softball,” said coach Gene Denard. “We gained some momentum and scored 16 runs. American is young like us, so it was a good opportunity for us.” It marked the second win of the season for freshman pitcher Talia Perl, who threw 99 pitches in five innings of work. She struck out six batters and allowed three earned runs. As a freshman Perl is at the start of what could be a strong pitching career at Piedmont High. The last time PHS featured a freshman thrower was Izzy Epstein, who was a fouryear starter from 2019-2022. She was the Post’s 2022 honorable mention for Athlete of the Year and won the WACC Shoreline’s Pitcher of the Year award. “I’ve been playing softball for eight years,” said Perl. :It’s crazy to think that I started off so young and I always watched the big girls play. Now I’m one of the older girls. I think I’m definitely getting more consistent,” 16-6 over American Down 2-0 entering the bottom of the second, Piedmont went ahead 3-2 after Perl drew a oneout walk, while she came around to score on multiple passed balls. With two outs, Penelope Hopper hit a single, then Makenna Small drew a walk. Elly Mak then an RBI double to score pinch runner Hailey Navarro and Small, who came in on an error. Piedmont’s nine-run third inning started with Hannah Joeger, Rosemary Dickinson, and Perl drawing three straight walks, then Kajsa Benson drawing a walk with the bases loaded. Hopper then hit a two-RBI single to score Perl and Dickinson. Mak drew another walk to load the bases, leading to Edie Elmquist also walking on five pitches to score Benson to make it 7-2. Teah Suhr grounded into a fielder’s choice to score Navarro, Joerger hit an RBI single to bring Mak around, while Dickinson hit a two-RBI single to make it 11-2—scoring Suhr and Elmquist. American inched back into the game, making it 12-4 after the top of the fifth, and 12-6 after its half of the sixth. articles.text: Local pro soccer team off to a 2-0-0 start Don’t look now, but Oakland might have a successful professional sports franchise. The Oakland Roots professional soccer team in the USL Championship hosted a near soldout crowd of 14,419 for its home opener on Saturday, March 14, selling 96 percent of its 15,000 capacity at the Coliseum. Roots won the match 2-1 over New Mexico United, improving its record to 2-0-0 and currently in first place in the Western Conference. Sports in the City of Oakland is a sore subject after the Raiders left for Las Vegas, the A’s departed for Sacramento and soon Las Vegas, while the Warriors moved across the bridge to San Francisco. 2026 marks the second year that Roots are playing at the Coliseum. For players and coaches on Roots, seeing such a crowd is unusual in the USL Championship, which is the second division of American professional soccer. “That was special for the league as a whole. The fans really represented Oakland as a sports town. It helped give our guys a little extra juice to close out the game. I was in awe of what I saw. I’ve seen a lot of crowded stadiums, but not one with the collective energy and the collective belief in the city and the club,” said Roots head coach Ryan Martin. Before the match, the team’s diehard supporters in the Deep Roots section unveiled a “tifo,” which is a customary large-scale, choreographed visual display produced by devout soccer fans in leagues all over the world. This year Roots’ supporters creOakland Roots’ Peter Wilson (left) and Neveal Hackshaw celebrate a goal in their 2-1 win over New Mexico United. ated an image of Marvel Comics’ Guardians of the Galaxy character, Groot, with the caption: “We Are Roots.” “The atmosphere was incredible. I just spoke to my girlfriend and some friends; they were all blown away. We’ve been together for a variety of stops, and this was by far the best we’ve been to. The crowd was really special. We definitely feed off their energy,” said team captain Tommy McCabe. Roots begin the season with new energy and starting its campaign 2-0-0 for the first time in club history under Martin. Oakland missed the playoffs last year after finishing 10th of 12 teams. They are in first place for the only time in the team’s six years in the league. The club has a strong roster, boasting 2025’s Golden Boot winner, Peter Wilson, leading the attack. Coach Martin, meanwhile, came to Oakland as the longest tenured coach in the league after spending 2019-2025 at Loudoun United in Virginia. He is approaching his 220th game as a manager. Through its first five years in the USL Championship, Roots never hired a head coach with previous experience in the league, showing a sign of change for the young organization. The highest Roots finished in the Western Conference was seventh in 2024. Should Oakland achieve a top-four spot, they would host their first-ever playoff game in November. As things look right now, momentum and the financial backing is finally on their side. Piedmont Post sports editor Jonathan Comeaux is also a beat reporter and insider covering Oakland Roots SC. articles.text: Play ends this Sunday American Conservatory Theater (A.C.T.) in San Francisco presents the North American premiere of Paranormal Activity, a new stage production based on the film franchise from Paramount Pictures, playing onstage now through Sunday, March 22. The new play presents an original story set in the world of the Paranormal Activity films created by filmmaker Oren Peli. The stage adaptation is written by Levi Holloway, whose credits include “Grey House,” and is conceived with director Felix Barrett. Illusions are designed by Tony Award winner Chris Fisher. The story follows James and Lou, who relocate from Chicago to London in an effort to leave their past behind. They encounter a series of unexplained events that suggest a continuing supernatural presence. Cher Álvarez and Patrick Heusinger star as Lou and James. Álvarez’s previous stage credits include work with Goodman Theatre, Steppenwolf Theatre and Writers Theatre. Heusinger has appeared on Broadway in Next Fall and Fiddler on the Roof. Shannon Cochran plays Carolanne, James’ mother, and Kate Fry portrays Etheline Cotgrave, a medium. Understudies are Caroline Hendricks, Michael Holding and Carol Buinis. articles.text: Opera San Jose closes its 2025/26 season with Verdi’s classic opera La Traviata, premiering Sunday, April 19. La Traviata is an opera in three acts by Giuseppe Verdi, based on the novel La Dame aux Camélias by Alexandre Dumas. Opera San Jose’s production includes Mikayla Sager, most recently seen as Mimì in La Bohème, as Violetta and former Opera San Jose Artist-in-Residence WooYoung Yoon as her young lover. Opera San Jose’s former Conductor in Residence Johannes Löhner returns to make his principal conducting debut with Director-in-Residence Tara Branham returning to direct La Traviata. Set in 19th-century Paris, it tells the tragic love story of the courtesan Violetta Valéry and the young nobleman Alfredo Germont. After meeting at a party, Alfredo confesses he has long loved Violetta. Though ill with tuberculosis and accustomed to a life of luxury and independence, she eventually falls in love with him. The two leave Paris to live together in the countryside. Their happiness is disrupted when Alfredo’s father, Giorgio Germont, asks Violetta to leave Alfredo. He argues that their scandalous relationship threatens his family’s reputation and his daughter’s marriage prospects. Mikayla Sager, most recently seen cast as the company’s Mimìs in La Bohème, is cast as Violetta in Opera San Jose’s production of La Traviata. Sacrificing her own happiness, Violetta secretly agrees and returns to her former life without explaining why. The opera will be performed onstage April 19 through May 3. Doors open 90 minutes before the performance, 12:30 p.m. for matinees and 6:00 p.m. for evening performances. May 1and 3 performances will be conducted by Conductor-in-Residence Noah Lindquist. A preshow discussion is held at 1:00 p.m. for matinees and 6:30 p.m. for evening performances. The organ player will be performing 30 minutes before curtain. Visit https://www.operasj.org/ productions/la-traviata to purchase tickets. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

articles.text: KAWS: FAMILY is on view at the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SFMOMA) now through May 3. KAWS: FAMILY presents more than 100 works spanning three decades of the artist KAWS’ (born Brian Donnelly, 1974) career. Organized by the Art Gallery of Ontario, the exhibition explores KAWS’ evolution from his early graffiti practice in Jersey City and Manhattan to a multidisciplinary career encompassing sculpture, painting, drawing, product design and large-scale public art. KAWS: FAMILY is the artist’s first major West Coast museum exhibition. “KAWS has a distinct appeal to a vast array of audiences with his iconic characters and meticulous work in a stunning range of mediums,” said Christopher Bedford, Helen and Charles Schwab Director of SFMOMA. “The playful and contemplative works, a dynamic blend of his street art practice and formal education, offer something for everyone. His large-scale public installations have wowed audiences worldwide, and his playful and poignant retrospective exhibition promises to connect museum visitors with art in entirely new ways.” KAWS’ work bridges consumer culture and fine art, working across multiple mediums, said Daryl McCurdy, curatorial associate of architecture and design and curator of KAWS: FAMILY at SFMOMA. “Though art history has tended to situate a critical divide between fine and commercial art, KAWS’s work across media and markets feels refreshingly indifferent to preconceived strata of aesthetic experience and art collecting,” McCurdy said. The San Francisco Museum of Modern Art is located at 151 Third St. in downtown San Francisco. Visit www.sfmoma.org for more information. KAWS’ work bridges consumer culture and fine art.

articles.text: So you’ve decided that you’d like to give conformation dog showing a try. The Beginner Puppy (B-Pup) competition is a fun way to test the waters when your puppy is between four and six months old. Although many individuals do not purchase puppies from breeders specifically to show them, your puppy may surprise you at their first competition. When attending your first show, bathe your puppy and brush them beforehand. Different breeds have different grooming requirements. Avoid any fancy haircuts or trimming until you know exactly how your breed is typically groomed for the show ring. Trim their nails, brush their teeth, and clean out their ears. Now you’re ready to pack! Don’t forget to bring your grooming materials, a crate and x-pen, and a source of shade. Days at dog shows can be very long, so bring supplies to keep yourself comfy as well, such as lawn chairs and a cooler. Plan to arrive early so that you have plenty of time to set up. Could be you’ll meet someone with the same breed who is willing to give you a few tips! Check the judges program so you know what time your puppy must be in the ring. Complete any last-minute grooming, then head over to get your armband number from the ring steward table, which is next to the ring. Don’t forget to potty your puppy on the way! To show your puppy, you will need a specific show lead and either slip collar or show chain. Vendors at the show can advise you on what to buy. Additionally, keep plenty of treats (bait) in your pocket. Your puppy will have to stack, meaning stand in a particular fashion that demonstrates their structure. Dogs with good structure can typically stack on their own without much help. Use your treat to keep your puppy’s eyes forward while the judge examines them. The judge may give you instructions such as showing them the bite (teeth), trotting the puppy down and back, or trotting the puppy all the way around the show ring. Keep your pace slow and listen to the judge for instructions. It could be your puppy will win a blue ribbon! If your puppy wins first place for their breed, stick around as they may have a chance to compete for best in show! Have fun, and don’t stress; both you and your puppy are learning. This is a great chance to practice while your puppy is still under six months old. You can also use the knowledge of where your puppy places to decide whether your dog has a show career ahead of them. Most of all, it’s an exciting way to bond with your dog! Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. articles.text: The Pardee Home Museum, a California Historical Landmark, an Oakland City Landmark, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places, dates to 1868. The home recently underwent a renovation restoring its historic character. Visitors can view the results during a reserved tour on Sunday, March 22, 2026, at 2 p.m., featuring a special lecture and guided tour by Steve and Lisa Bauer of Bradbury & Bradbury. At 158 years old, the home has witnessed and contributed to both Oakland and California history. Over time, it has endured earthquakes, roof leaks and the natural settling that comes with age. While the first-floor interior was painted in recent years, the second-floor wall coverings had not been updated since the 1950s. The upstairs rooms required careful attention before any cosmetic work could begin. Preservation efforts focused on maintaining historical accuracy while addressing structural needs. To find an appropriate design, the museum partnered with the Bradbury & Bradbury Wallpaper Company, now based in Sacramento. The firm agreed to assist with the restoration, bringing expertise in historically accurate designs. Steve Bauer, owner of Bradbury & Bradbury, researched wallpaper styles from the late 1800s and created coordinated designs for the walls and ceilings of three bedrooms and the billiard room. One of the custom patterns developed for the project is now included in the company’s international catalog as “The Pardee.” Wallpaper installer Joel Lucas was hired to complete the work. The project required extensive wall repair and preparation before installation Master Bedroom - Before Photos courtesy of Pardee Home Museum Madeline’s Bedroom - Before Master Bedroom - After Madeline’s Bedroom - After could begin. Over four months, Lucas restored the surfaces and applied the custom designs. The result is a carefully executed restoration that reflects the home’s original elegance. With the project complete, the Pardee Home Museum continues to preserve its legacy while offering visitors a glimpse into its renewed historic interiors. The photos show much of the process, but a visit will truly show the magnificence of the finished project. articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently held their monthly meeting with four distinguished Piedmont City employees attending to address the group regarding the latest city improvements. They included Communications Program Manager Echa Schneider, Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The core of the conversation revolved around the modernizing of Piedmont’s emergency response. The Police Department lobby re-opened recently following the completion of its new 9-1-1 dispatch center. It is Piedmont’s most significant public safety investment in decades. Previously, the nearly 80-year-old Police Department building was powered by a 200-amp electrical panel – a capacity more typical of a single family home than a 24/7 public safety facility – and lacked dedicated backup power. Now, this latest project has delivered a modern electrical core designed for today’s public safety operations, including secure, independent backup power, ensuring that the Police Department and dispatch center can remain operational during extended power outrages or major emergencies. While the 9-1-1 dispatch center replacement is one of an unprecedented number of capital projects completed, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales spoke about other significant infrastructure investments including Piedmont’s streets, storm drains, and a new sanitary sewer system. There will be an upgrade in street maintenance, sidewalks, street lighting, signage, and provisions to promote pedestrian and bicycle safety, as well as public landscaping and street tree maintenance. Fire Chief Dave Brannigan then spoke of helping the community prepare for emergencies as well as educating the community about fire prevention and disaster preparedness. With the recent upgrades to the system, the Piedmont Fire Department will now be better able to provide the community with comprehensive and superior emergency services to protect life, property, and the environment. It was a most educational day for all who attended. After the meeting a catered lunch was served to the delight of all. If you would like to find out more information about the Piedmont Seniors program, contact Janet Epstein, coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. The Seniors meet monthly on Wednesday mornings from 10 to noon at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, in addition to going on monthly excursions throughout the Bay Area. Featured speakers at the recent Piedmont Seniors’ monthly meeting included: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales (left), Police Chief Frederick Shavies, Fire Chief Dave Brannigan, Piedmont Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, and Communications Program Director Echa Schneider.

articles.text: Allyson Huynh Weavers is a new community program designed to connect Piedmont seniors with local teens for companionship, support, and meaningful conversation. Founded by sophomores Luca LaForte and Allyson Huynh, Weavers pairs seniors with members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew to help reduce isolation and strengthen intergenerational ties. The spring pilot will match 15 seniors with 15 student volunteers. Pairs will meet once a week over a six-week period, with the option to continue together or be rematched at the end of the program. Visits may include conversation, light household assistance, or simply spending time together. The program is open to Piedmont seniors who would enjoy regular connection with younger generations. Families and caregivers are also encouraged to reach out on behalf of interested participants. articles.text: I’m sorting this out in real time. This may not be the most uplifting column I’ve written, but it may be one of the most important. Not all of us have children nearby or family members able to step in as caregivers. Because of that reality, each of us must take responsibility for planning our future as we enter the golden years and beyond. Preparation deserves the same care we give to planning a vacation. You wouldn’t show up at the airport without a passport, a ticket, or a destination. Yet many people do exactly that when it comes to aging. Create a checklist. Identify the people who can support you. Think about where you might live in the future the same way you would research a hotel for a stay in a new city. When you plan ahead, you give yourself options and a softer landing. When you don’t, decisions are often made during a crisis. As I often say in Mindset in Motion, if you fail to plan, you are planning to fail. Jackie’s story Jackie’s story has brought that lesson into focus. Not long ago, Jackie fell. She lives in an independent living community, not assisted living. That distinction matters. Independent living offers housing and community, but not the medical or daily support someone may suddenly need after an accident. Even though it was “just a fall,” she was taken to the hospital by ambulance. Twice. If Jackie had close family nearby, someone might have driven her to urgent care or called her doctor. Instead, the system responded the way it is designed to. She was transported to the hospital. Because she could not get downstairs for meals she returned again. A hospital, however, is not long-term care. When someone has no strong support system, it can become a temporary place of refuge. Soon after, she was discharged to a rehabilitation facility. On the surface it looked like a quiet residential building, but inside it felt more like an extension of the hospital. Jackie spent long hours in bed. When I visited, her room was dark and she needed help simply getting to the bathroom. Her hip was sore from the fall, but days of inactivity caused new pain as well. Communication about her care was inconsistent. The evening nurse said physical therapy happened daily, Jackie begged to differ. Who was telling the truth? While I was away for two days, Jackie was discharged and sent home in a truck she barely remembers. She was so embarrassed she covered her head with a borrowed scarf. Moments like this highlight the limits of friendship in situations requiring professional care. I am not Jackie’s nurse or family member. I am a friend and neighbor doing my best to help. During this process I also learned that many of Jackie’s behaviors—frustration, forgetfulness, and sudden anger—may be signs of cognitive decline. Hearing that was difficult, but it explained much of the confusion. Months ago, Jackie gave me four phone numbers written on a small piece of paper for her fiduciary, attorney, a niece three states over whom I have never met, and the Neptune Society. I mentioned to Jackie that she should speak with her fiduciary, but she kept repeating that he is not needed until she passes. That isn’t accurate, yet she continues to resist the idea. He did explain that he could coordinate care and help manage important decisions if she asked him to step in. However, Jackie emphatically denies that this is part of his role. At the moment, we are at a standstill. He does have a copy of her trust and all the important paperwork in his possession for when the time comes. Just seven months ago we celebrated her move into independent living. Now we are preparing for the possibility of assisted living. Aging can change quickly. Jackie’s story is a reminder for all of us to ask ourselves a few important questions. Do you have a plan? Do you have trusted people who know your wishes? Have you prepared legally and financially for the years ahead? Planning for aging is not about fear. It is about dignity, choice, and control. The best time to create a plan is long before you need one. DiMaggio Betta Group, Corcoran Icon Properties, 510.414.6777, Debbi.DiMaggio@ corcoranicon.com

By Cookie Segelstein Dear MacMama, Even though my laptop is only two years old, I decided I am finding it just too hard to work and see the 13-inch screen. So, I want to get the larger one. I know Apple offers a trade in, but I wonder if there are better places to sell it. Apple only offers $650 dollars for my MacBook Air, and I paid over $2000 three years ago. Also, once I am ready, how do I remove all my information and get the computer ready for sale? James, Oakland Dear James, I’m going to answer your second question first; how to get your laptop ready for sale or to give away. Since your laptop is only two years old, even if you have not updated your operating system, you have the option to do an easy erase and reset with the “erase all content” option in System Settings. Any mac with at least Ventura (released in 2022) has this option. Here are the steps to do this: 1. Click on the Apple in the upper left of your screen and choose “System Settings”. 2. Click on “General” in the sidebar on the left. 3. Scroll down on the right until you see “Transfer or Reset”. 4. Click “Erase all content and settings”. 5. When the erase window comes up, you will be asked to sign in with your administrative credentials (NOT your Apple ID, your computer account, which is usually your name), and then put in your computer password. 6. You then might be asked if you want to back up your Mac with Time Machine, which you should have done before you started this process. 7. Then you will see a summary of all the things that will be erased, which will only affect the machine you are erasing. 8. You will also be asked to sign out of iCloud with your Apple ID and password, which should also disable Find My Mac (I disable Find My Mac and sign out of iCloud before I start the whole process). 9. Click the Erase All Content & Settings button. Your Mac will restart and be in “Recovery”mode, and you must activate it, which you do by clicking on the Wi-Fi signal in the upper right and joining your WIFI network. Once activated, it is in “out of the box” state, and ready for a new owner. Before you do all of this, as I said earlier, you should make sure you have a backup of your data, if you plan to use Time Machine to set up a new laptop. Other things you must do is sign out of any subscription software like Microsoft Office, Adobe products like Photoshop or Lightroom, or any software that uses licensing to control how many installations you can have. These licenses are often tied to your machine with a system ID, and if you forget to do this on certain software, it can be very difficult to get the license moved over. Also making sure that “find my Mac” is turned off, prevents the machine from being in your list of devices in your iCloud account even when it eventually belongs to somebody else. Let’s talk about some other places you can sell your machine. The best thing is a personal sale; someone you know who is looking for a used but current computer. Of course you must determine what your computer is worth. And for that, you could look at some of the online sales sites like, eBay or even Facebook marketplace. One of my favorite places to sell used devices is swappa.com, as they do not charge a commission, and the fee to sell is very low. To determine a price, look at the for-sale section and search for the specifics of your machine. You can also find prices on resale sites like mac2sell.net, itsworthmore. com, and sellyourmac.com. The downside of these online sites, as you have to arrange to ship your machine. That’s why I think that Facebook marketplace as I mentioned above is also a good place to sell locally. You would also be surprised, that if you start telling people that you have a two-yearold laptop for sale, you will often find someone interested. You can also use Craigslist, of course, but you have to be very careful about making sure potential buyers are legitimate. Craigslist is usually my last resort for electronics. Some people just do the apple trade-in because it’s convenient, but very likely your machine is worth a few hundred dollars more than Apple will offer you. This may not be the most uplifting column I’ve written, but it may be one of the most important. Not all of us have children nearby or family members able to step in as caregivers. Because of that reality, each of us must take responsibility for planning our future as we enter the golden years and beyond. Preparation deserves the same care we give to planning a vacation. You wouldn’t show up at the airport without a passport, a ticket, or a destination. Yet many people do exactly that when it comes to aging. Create a checklist. Identify the people who can support you. Think about where you might live in the future the same way you would research a hotel for a stay in a new city. When you plan ahead, you give yourself options and a softer landing. When you don’t, decisions are often made during a crisis. As I often say in Mindset in Motion, if you fail to plan, you are planning to fail. Jackie’s story Jackie’s story has brought that lesson into focus. Not long ago, Jackie fell. She lives in an independent living community, not assisted living. That distinction matters. Independent living offers housing and community, but not the medical or daily support someone may suddenly need after an accident. Even though it was “just a fall,” she was taken to the hospital by ambulance. Twice. If Jackie had close family nearby, someone might have driven her to urgent care or called her doctor. Instead, the system responded the way it is designed to. She was transported to the hospital. Because she could not get downstairs for meals she returned again. A hospital, however, is not long-term care. When someone has no strong support system, it can become a temporary place of refuge. Soon after, she was discharged to a rehabilitation facility. On the surface it looked like a quiet residential building, but inside it felt more like an extension of the hospital. Jackie spent long hours in bed. When I visited, her room was dark and she needed help simply getting to the bathroom. Her hip was sore from the fall, but days of inactivity caused new pain as well. Communication about her care was inconsistent. The evening nurse said physical therapy happened daily, Jackie begged to differ. Who was telling the truth? While I was away for two days, Jackie was discharged and sent home in a truck she barely remembers. She was so embarrassed she covered her head with a borrowed scarf. Moments like this highlight the limits of friendship in situations requiring professional care. I am not Jackie’s nurse or family member. I am a friend and neighbor doing my best to help. During this process I also learned that many of Jackie’s behaviors—frustration, forgetfulness, and sudden anger—may be signs of cognitive decline. Hearing that was difficult, but it explained much of the confusion. Months ago, Jackie gave me four phone numbers written on a small piece of paper for her fiduciary, attorney, a niece three states over whom I have never met, and the Neptune Society. I mentioned to Jackie that she should speak with her fiduciary, but she kept repeating that he is not needed until she passes. That isn’t accurate, yet she continues to resist the idea. He did explain that he could coordinate care and help manage important decisions if she asked him to step in. However, Jackie emphatically denies that this is part of his role. At the moment, we are at a standstill. He does have a copy of her trust and all the important paperwork in his possession for when the time comes. Just seven months ago we celebrated her move into independent living. Now we are preparing for the possibility of assisted living. Aging can change quickly. Jackie’s story is a reminder for all of us to ask ourselves a few important questions. Do you have a plan? Do you have trusted people who know your wishes? articles.text: When I was asked: “did you like the music?” a famous story helped me. This is how I answered the question. When George Frederick Handel was a young composer living in Italy, he heard that one of his pieces was to be performed. He would attend the rehearsal and concert conducted by one of the greatest musicians of all time, Arcangelo Corelli. As Handel listened to the rehearsal, he became agitated by Corelli’s inability to play Handel’s music. He finally walked up to Corelli and took his violin and said: “THIS is how my music should be played. Do you understand?” Corelli was embarrassed to say the least. He responded very diplomatically by saying: “I’m sorry. I just don’t understand MODERN music.” It seems that differences of opinion make music as well as horse racing. We must keep an open mind. Music and adventure are virtually synonymous. And the adventure continues.

articles.text: It is intended to be a time of repentance, prayer, fasting, self-discipline, charity and giving. Many people give up something for Lent, like cookies or beer. There are charming stories of children - not quite clear on the concept - saying they will give up making their beds or eating Brussels sprouts. Lent begins on Ash Wednesday, which falls 40 days before Easter. This year Ash Wednesday was February 18. In many places, the day before Ash Wednesday is a day of feasting and partying before the more sober period of Lent begins. It is called Mardi Gras, Carnival or Fat Tuesday. On Ash Wednesday, Christians go to church and receive ashes on their foreheads in the shape of a cross, symbolizing mortality, repentance and a time of spiritual reflection. The last week of Lent is Holy Week, which begins with Palm Sunday. On this Sunday, Christians celebrate Jesus’ triumphal entrance into Jerusalem even as it foreshadowed the coming Last Supper, Crucifixion and Resurrection. These events are celebrated on Maundy Thursday, Good Friday and Easter Sunday, respectively. Christians receive ashes on their foreheads on Ash Wednesday to symbolize death, repentance and a desire to live in Christ’s image. Unlike Christmas, which is always on December 25, Easter - the most important celebration in Christianity - falls between March 22 and April 25.The actual date is determined by solar and lunar timing as it is the first Sunday after the first full moon that occurs on or after the March 21 Spring equinox. This formula was established by the Council of Nicea (AD 325) and ties loosely to Jewish Passover, since that is when scripture says the crucifixion and resurrection occurred. This year Easter falls on April 5. Lent is a 40-day period of preparation leading up to Easter. The 40 days reflects the 40 days that Jesus spent in the wilderness before beginning his ministry. 2026 LENTEN SERVICES Palm Sunday, March 29 at 10am Maundy Thursday, April 2 at 6pm Good Friday, April 3 at 7:30pm Easter Sunday, April 5 at 8:30 and 10am
